title: One vehicle (Kern ch. 2)
hookLine: the three vehicles were skillful means; really there is one vehicle to Buddhahood for all

cards: Three travelers board a train through three different doors: front, middle and back. Each settles in and thinks of it as their own car. Then the conductor walks through and says: it's one train, going to one station.
The doors were only so you could all get on. That's roughly the moment chapter two of the Lotus Sutra builds to, and it unsettles some of the people who had been walking longest.

teach.b: Buddhist teaching speaks of different paths called vehicles, yana in Sanskrit, the word for a cart or carriage.
The Lotus names three: the vehicle of the disciples who hear the teaching, the vehicle of those who awaken on their own, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. Different travelers, different carts.

Then, in chapter two, the Buddha tells Sariputra plainly: there is only one vehicle, the Buddha-vehicle. Not a second, not a third. The three were skillful means, offered because people differ in what they can hear.
Underneath them the destination is the same for everyone: Buddhahood itself. That is ekayana, the one vehicle. And the sutra keeps widening the door, almost playfully.

In Kern's translation the Buddha describes people who once made a small offering at a shrine, or bowed, or raised a hand, or said a single word of honor to the Buddha, even children who piled up sand as a stupa while they played.
All of them, the sutra says, have reached awakening. The vehicle has room for the child in the sandbox. In the sutra's own story this is not a soft message.
It tells disciples who had worked hard toward their own goal that the goal was a stopping place, not the end.

teach.h: SCHOOLS READ IT THEIR OWN WAY.

teach.b: Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren teachers put the one vehicle at the center of their teaching. The Lotus is not part of the Theravada canon, and Theravada teachers describe the path in their own terms.
Today simply hears what the Lotus says, in its own voice. Tomorrow it becomes a story: a house, a fire, some children, and carts.

how: In the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools the one vehicle of the Lotus Sutra is a central teaching, studied as the meaning beneath all the Buddha's other teachings; Theravada Buddhists do not use the Lotus Sutra as scripture.

o: a cart that carries monks between monasteries
the single rule every Buddhist school agrees on
the one vehicle: every path leads to Buddhahood

p: a play stupa, and room in the vehicle

s: the Lotus Sutra says the three vehicles lead to three different goals
it says the three were skillful means; there is one vehicle, to Buddhahood.
the sutra mentions children who pile up sand as a stupa while playing
it is one of its examples of small acts that the Buddha says lead to awakening.
every Buddhist school treats the Lotus Sutra as scripture
Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools center it; Theravada Buddhists do not use it as scripture.

games.q: you have spent years on the disciples' path toward your own release. the Buddha says there is only one vehicle. what does that mean for your goal?
o: it was the wrong path all along
it was a resting place, and the road goes on to Buddhahood
games.why: in the Lotus the earlier paths were skillful means, not mistakes; the one vehicle carries everyone further, to Buddhahood itself.

practice: Picture a few people who look for meaning in very different ways: one who prays, one who runs, one who paints, one who simply cares for others.
Let each picture rest a moment, and without deciding anything about them, ask quietly what they might be walking toward. If no answer comes, just rest in the question.

wordCard.voice: Ekayana. The one vehicle: in the Lotus Sutra, the teaching that the many paths were skillful means, and all of them carry to the same awakening. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: eka, one, plus yana, vehicle; the Lotus Sutra's one Buddha-vehicle.

carryVoice: Your line: one vehicle. Three doors, one train. Back tomorrow, same hill.
